system.disclosure: SafeMan™ is a proprietary inter-organizational safety management and operational competency benchmark developed by Oryx Institute (safeman.oryxinstitute.org). Courses are engineered in alignment with ISO 45001:2018, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 31000, ILO-OSH guidelines, and pre-referenced against Namibia Training Authority (NTA) Unit Standards and Namibian Government Notice 156 of 1997 for corporate audit readiness. SafeMan credentials verify industry competency and attendance between organizations and are non-NQA credit-bearing.

modules.title: Why safety management exists
modules.focus: The moral, legal and business case for managed safety, and how ISO 45001:2018 structures an occupational health and safety system through its high-level architecture.
keypoints: ISO 45001:2018 follows the harmonized structure: context (Cl.4), leadership (Cl.5), planning (Cl.6), support (Cl.7), operation (Cl.8), evaluation (Cl.9), improvement (Cl.10).
Work-related injury and ill health are preventable; a managed system makes prevention routine rather than lucky.
Under Namibia's Labour Act 11 of 2007 the employer carries the primary duty of care; workers carry duties to cooperate and to report.
Cost of loss goes beyond medical bills: lost time, retraining, reputational damage and statutory exposure.

modules.title: The PDCA safety cycle
modules.focus: Plan-Do-Check-Act as the operating rhythm of every ISO management system, mapped to the clauses a SafeMan practitioner will touch daily.
keypoints: Plan: context, interested parties, OH&S risks and opportunities, objectives (Cl.4 and Cl.6).
Do: resources, competence, communication, operational control, emergency preparedness (Cl.7–8).
Check: monitoring, measurement, internal audit, management review inputs (Cl.9).
Act: nonconformity, corrective action, continual improvement (Cl.10).

modules.title: Hazard classes and duty of care
modules.focus: The major hazard families found on Namibian workplaces and the legal duty of care that attaches to every level of the organization.
keypoints: Hazard families: physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychosocial, and safety-mechanical.
GN 156 of 1997 (Regulations relating to the Health and Safety of Employees at Work) sets the working rules: first aid, PPE, machinery, confined spaces, noise and more.
Duty of care under Labour Act 11 of 2007: safe plant, safe systems, information, training, supervision, PPE at employer's cost.
Personal risk accountability: every worker owns the rule to stop unsafe work and report what cannot be controlled.

modules.title: Personal risk accountability
modules.focus: Closing the sprint: the SafeMan personal discipline — task risk check, stop-work authority, and reporting that actually changes the workplace.
keypoints: Before any task: what can hurt me, who else, and what has changed since the plan was written?
Stop-work authority is exercised respectfully and without fear of reprisal; a stopped job is a paid job.
Reports that name the hazard, the location and the proposed fix get closed out; reports that only complain do not.
Your SafeMan ticket is a personal record: keep it current, verify it with the QR code, know its expiry.

quiz.q: Which clause of ISO 45001:2018 deals with the 'Context of the organization'?
quiz.why: Clause 4 covers context, interested parties and the scope of the OH&S management system.

quiz.q: The primary legal duty of care for workplace safety in Namibia rests with the:
quiz.why: Labour Act 11 of 2007 places the primary duty on the employer; employees must cooperate and report.

quiz.q: Plan-Do-Check-Act: where do internal audits sit?
quiz.why: Audits are evaluation activities in the Check phase (Cl. 9).

o: Health and Safety of Employees at Work regulations
quiz.why: GN 156 of 1997 contains the working regulations: first aid, PPE, machinery, confined spaces, noise.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the five hazard families taught in this sprint?
quiz.why: The taught families are physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic and psychosocial; financial risk is not an OH&S hazard class.

quiz.q: The correct response on finding an uncontrolled hazard you cannot fix is to:
o: Wait for the shift to end
quiz.why: Stop-work and report: a hazard nobody owns becomes an incident.

quiz.q: PPE under Namibian law is provided:
quiz.why: The employer provides PPE at its own cost as part of the duty of care.
Planning (Cl. 6) covers risks, opportunities, objectives; the others are Check/Act.
SafeMan is a proprietary inter-organizational benchmark; it is non-NQA credit-bearing.

quiz.q: 'Operational control' belongs to which ISO 45001 clause?
quiz.why: Operation — including operational control and emergency preparedness — is Clause 8.

quiz.q: The cheapest and most effective point in the hierarchy of controls is:
quiz.why: Elimination removes the hazard entirely and always outranks controls that only reduce exposure.
Psychosocial hazards act on the mind: violence, bullying, workload, fatigue.

quiz.q: Management review is an input-output loop that:
quiz.why: Management review (Cl. 9.3) judges whether the system is suitable, adequate and effective.

quiz.q: A near-miss should be reported because:
o: It is free information about failure of control
quiz.why: A near-miss is a free rehearsal of a real incident; the failed control is already known.

quiz.q: SafeMan PDCA discipline says corrective action must:
quiz.why: Corrective action that does not reach root cause buys the same incident twice.

modules.title: ISO 45001:2018 Architecture, Context & Leadership (Cl. 4–5)
modules.focus: The clause-by-clause skeleton of an OH&S management system and what leadership must visibly own for the system to function.
keypoints: Clause 4: external/internal issues, workers and other interested parties, scope of the system.
Clause 5: leadership and worker consultation — policy, roles, responsibilities and authorities documented and visible.
The system must be integrated into business processes, not bolted on as a safety file on a shelf.
Top management demonstrates commitment with resources, protection of workers from reprisal, and participation structures.

modules.title: ISO 31000 Risk Architecture, Baseline/Issue-Based HIRA & BowTie
modules.focus: Enterprise risk principles applied to OH&S: baseline, issue-based and continuous risk assessment, and barrier thinking with BowTie diagrams.
keypoints: ISO 31000 process: communication, scope/context/criteria, risk assessment (identification, analysis, evaluation), treatment, monitoring, recording.
Three assessment types: baseline (whole operation), issue-based (new plant, change, incident), continuous (task and pre-use checks).
BowTie: hazard on the knot, threats left, consequences right, preventive and mitigative barriers drawn as lines of defence.
Every barrier needs an owner, a performance standard and a checking routine, or it is decoration.

modules.title: Operational Control — Safe Systems of Work, e-PTW & Contractor SHE Vetting
modules.focus: Converting risk assessment into rules people actually follow: safe systems of work, electronic permit-to-work and the contractor SHE file gate.
keypoints: A safe system of work = task analysis, written method, competence check, supervision, and a review trigger.
PTW is required for high-hazard work: hot work, confined space, electrical isolation, excavation, working at heights.
An electronic PTW adds conflict detection: the system refuses two permits that fight each other.
Contractor SHE vetting gate: safety file, medicals, competence records, insurance, and a site induction before the first spanner turns.

modules.title: ISO 14001:2015 Environmental Management, Aspect/Impact & Spill Control
modules.focus: Environmental side of the SHEQ function: aspects and impacts registers, operational control, and first-response spill containment.
keypoints: Aspect = how your activity touches the environment; impact = the change in the environment.
Significance scoring uses severity, duration, frequency and legal exposure; significant aspects get controls and objectives.
Emergency spills: contain at source, protect drains, notify per the site plan, dispose as hazardous waste with a manifest.
Waste hierarchy: avoid, reduce, reuse, recycle, treat, dispose.

modules.title: Occupational Hygiene — Exposure Limits (TWA/STEL) & Hierarchy of Controls
modules.focus: Anticipation, recognition, evaluation and control of workplace health stressors, with the 8-hour TWA and STEL concepts done properly.
keypoints: Occupational hygiene survey cycle: anticipate, recognize, evaluate, control.
TWA averages exposure over a reference shift (8 h); STEL caps short peaks (typically 15 min); ceilings are never-exceed values.
Controls in order: elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE — PPE is the last line, not the first.
Health stressors: dust (incl. silica), noise, vibration, heat, radiation, chemicals, biological agents.

modules.title: Emergency Preparedness, Fire Engineering & Crisis Command
modules.focus: Building an emergency capability that survives contact with a real event: plans, equipment, command structure and drills.
keypoints: Emergency plan elements: identified scenarios, alarm and communication, roles (incident controller, marshals, first aiders), assembly, roll call, handover to authorities.
Fire engineering basics: ignition source, fuel, oxidizer — remove any leg of the tetrahedron and the fire fails.
Crisis command: one voice, one board, timed decisions, a log kept from the first minute.
Drills are assessed against time objectives (e.g. full evacuation), not just performed for a photo.

modules.title: ICAM Incident Investigation, Root-Cause Taxonomy & Cost of Loss
modules.focus: Investigating for system failure rather than blame: the ICAM framework, evidence handling and the real cost of loss arithmetic.
keypoints: ICAM layers: organizational influences, planning and supervision, task/environment conditions, individual/team actions, and the absent or failed defences.
Evidence first: scene, positions, people, parts, papers — before memories converge and the scene is cleaned.
Root-cause taxonomy distinguishes immediate causes (energy, substance) from contributing conditions and underlying organizational factors.
Direct cost (injury, damage) is the tip; indirect cost (downtime, investigation, retraining, reputation) typically runs multiples higher.

modules.title: ISO 19011 Internal HSE Auditing, Non-Conformance Grading & Management Review
modules.focus: Auditing the system against its own claims: audit programme, evidence grading, findings that drive improvement, and closing the loop at management review.
keypoints: Audit programme: scope, criteria, frequency by risk, auditor independence, documented method.
Evidence: objective trails (records, observations, interviews) traced against clauses — opinions are not findings.
Grade non-conformities: major (system failure or legal breach), minor (isolated lapse), observation (improvement signal).
Findings feed corrective action with owners and dates, and their trend feeds management review.

quiz.q: ISO 45001 Clause 5 requires top management to:
o: Delegate safety to the safety officer
Demonstrate leadership and protect workers from reprisal
quiz.why: Leadership means visible ownership, resources, and a culture where raising concerns carries no retaliation.

quiz.q: A BowTie diagram's knot represents the:
quiz.why: The hazard sits on the knot: threats on the left, consequences on the right, barriers as the bow.

quiz.q: Which risk assessment type responds to a new machine installation?
quiz.why: Issue-based assessments are triggered by change: new plant, process, people or after incidents.

quiz.q: In ISO 31000, risk treatment options include all EXCEPT:
o: Hiding the risk from the register
quiz.why: Risk registers are honest records; concealment is not a treatment option.

o: An owner and a performance standard
quiz.why: A barrier without an owner and standard decays silently until it fails.

o: At task level, before and during work
quiz.why: Continuous assessment is the working habit: pre-task checks and changing-condition reviews.

quiz.q: An electronic permit-to-work adds most value by:
quiz.why: e-PTW systems block incompatible simultaneous work — hot work beside a flammable vent, for example.

quiz.q: Before a contractor's first shift, the host must verify:
o: A complete SHE file, medicals and site induction
quiz.why: The contractor gate: safety file, competence and medical fitness, then induction.

quiz.q: A safe system of work fails fastest when:
quiz.why: Systems decay where supervision stops checking practice against the written method.

o: How an activity interacts with the environment
quiz.why: Aspect is the interaction (e.g. diesel storage); impact is the resulting change (e.g. soil contamination).

quiz.q: First response to a chemical spill is to:
o: Contain at source and protect drains
quiz.why: Contain at source, stop entry to drains and watercourses, then clean up per the plan.

quiz.q: The waste hierarchy's first preference is:
quiz.why: Avoid and reduce first; disposal is the last resort.

o: Health effects track accumulated dose over a reference shift
quiz.why: Dose over the reference shift drives chronic health effects; TWA standardizes the comparison.
Short-Term Exposure Limits cap brief peaks (commonly 15 minutes) that could injure quickly.
Controls decrease in reliability as you descend; PPE is the last line.

quiz.q: Silica dust is principally dangerous because it:
o: Causes irreversible scarring of lung tissue (silicosis)
quiz.why: Respirable crystalline silica scars the lungs — silicosis — and raises cancer risk.

quiz.q: The fire tetrahedron's four sides are:
quiz.why: Fuel, oxygen, heat and the ongoing chemical chain reaction.
A drill without timing and assessment is theatre, not preparedness.

quiz.q: The incident controller in a crisis:
o: Runs a single command board with a log
quiz.why: One command voice, a decision log from minute one, structured handover to authorities.
ICAM digs to organizational influences — the decisions that set everyone up to fail or succeed.

quiz.q: First investigation evidence to secure is:
o: The scene, positions, people, parts and papers
quiz.why: Scene, positions, people, parts, papers — before the scene changes and memories converge.

o: Run at multiples of direct costs
quiz.why: Downtime, investigation, replacement, retraining and reputation usually cost multiples of the direct bill.

quiz.q: A major non-conformity in an audit means:
quiz.why: Major = the system is broken or the law breached; minor = isolated lapse; observation = improvement signal.

o: A certified lead auditor for internal audits
quiz.why: Independence — you cannot objectively audit work you own or performed.

quiz.q: Audit findings are valid when based on:
quiz.why: Findings trace evidence against audit criteria: records, observation, interviews.
Cl. 9.3 asks three questions: is it suitable, adequate, effective — and what must change.

quiz.q: Worker consultation under ISO 45001 must be:
o: Once a year at the party
Structured and two-way on OH&S matters
quiz.why: Cl. 5.4 requires mechanisms for consultation and participation of workers at all levels.

o: Internal/external issues and interested parties relevant to OH&S
quiz.why: Issues and interested parties — workers, regulators, contractors, communities — that affect or are affected by OH&S.
Cl. 6.2: objectives measurable, with actions, resources, responsibilities and timeframes.
Significance drives control and improvement — that is the point of the register.

o: It removes the hazard instead of reducing exposure
quiz.why: A removed hazard cannot reach the worker when a mask fails or a filter is expired.

quiz.q: Heat stress controls include all EXCEPT:
quiz.why: Piece-rate pressure worsens heat exposure; the rest are standard controls.

quiz.q: A near-miss differs from an incident because:
o: It caused no injury or damage this time
quiz.why: Same failed controls, zero consequence this time — free information.

o: Scheduled assurance checks against the standard
quiz.why: Barriers need scheduled verification against their performance standard, or they rot.

quiz.q: In contractor management, the site induction happens:
quiz.why: No induction, no site — the induction is the last gate before work.

quiz.q: Documented information under ISO 45001 must be:
o: Controlled, current and available where needed
quiz.why: Control what matters, where it is needed; volume is not a virtue.

quiz.q: Workers must be consulted on OH&S matters because:
o: Cl. 5.4 makes participation a system requirement
quiz.why: ISO 45001 Cl. 5.4 requires consultation and participation mechanisms for workers.

quiz.q: The scope statement of an OH&S system defines:
o: What activities, sites and functions the system covers
quiz.why: Cl. 4.3 scopes the system so audits and controls match reality.

o: Planned responses, training, drills and periodic testing
quiz.why: Response plans are planned, resourced, practised and tested — then revised.

quiz.q: A documented information control exists mainly to:
o: Keep records current, protected and available where needed
quiz.why: Control ensures the right version is in the right hands at the point of use.

courses.title: SafeMan Basic Life Support, CPR & Choking Responder
courses.subtitle: Theory + Manikin Practicum

modules.title: Chain of survival & scene safety
modules.focus: The out-of-hospital chain of survival and making yourself the second casualty's prevention, not its cause.
keypoints: Chain: early recognition and call, early CPR, early defibrillation, advanced care, post-arrest care.
Scene check: hazards to self, bystanders, then the casualty — electricity, traffic, gas, water, machinery.
DRABC: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, CPR/Circulation.
Send a specific person for the AED: point, name, task.

modules.title: Adult CPR 30:2 & AED
modules.focus: Compression mechanics at 100–120 per minute with a 30:2 cycle, and safe, fast AED use.
keypoints: Centre of chest, 5–6 cm depth, full recoil, 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
Rate 100–120/min — the beat of classic disco tempo, not faster.
AED: power on, pads per diagrams, clear for analysis, clear before shock, resume immediately after.
Two-minute cycles; swap compressors at cycles to protect quality.

modules.title: Choking & recovery position
modules.focus: Airway obstruction grades and the escalation from cough encouragement to back blows and abdominal thrusts, then the recovery position.
keypoints: Mild obstruction: encourage coughing, stay with them.
Severe obstruction: 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating.
Unconscious choking casualty: lower to floor, start CPR.
Recovery position: airway open, stable, monitored — head tilted, knee braced, face toward the ground.

quiz.why: 100–120 compressions per minute balances filling time against circulation.
At least 5 cm, not more than 6 cm, with full recoil between compressions.
30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths for lay-responder adult CPR.

quiz.q: First action on reaching a collapsed casualty:
quiz.why: DRABC starts with D — you cannot help anyone as the second casualty.

quiz.q: Before the AED analyses rhythm you must:
quiz.why: Clear for analysis and clear for shock — movement corrupts the rhythm reading and the shock must not travel.

o: 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts
quiz.why: Back blows first; alternate with abdominal thrusts while the obstruction persists.
An effective cough clears more than interference does; stay ready to escalate.

quiz.q: If a choking casualty becomes unconscious:
o: Lower to floor and start CPR
quiz.why: CPR maintains circulation and the compressions also generate airway pressure.

o: Keeping the airway open and drainage safe
quiz.why: It protects the airway of a breathing, unresponsive casualty and lets fluid drain.
Recognition/call, CPR, defibrillation, advanced care, post-arrest care.

o: Centre of the chest, lower half of the sternum
quiz.why: Centre of the chest on the lower half of the sternum, heels of hands stacked.
Quality decays with fatigue long before the rescuer feels tired.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Basic Life Support
practicum.pass_standard: All steps signed off by a qualified assessor on a manikin.
steps: Scene hazard check performed and gloves donned before contact.
2-minute continuous chest compression and rescue-breath cycle on manikin at 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil.
Safe AED pad application with clear-for-analysis and clear-for-shock calls made audibly.
Choking back-blows and abdominal thrust technique demonstrated on the trainer vest.
Casualty placed correctly in the recovery position with airway maintained.

courses.title: SafeMan Workplace First Aid Responder (Level 1 Equivalent)
courses.subtitle: Theory + Practical Drills

modules.title: Statutory kit & secondary survey
modules.focus: What GN 156 expects in a workplace first aid kit and the head-to-toe secondary survey once life threats are controlled.
keypoints: Kit per GN 156 Reg. 228: sterile dressings, bandages, cleansing, gloves, mouthpiece, first aid manual, incident register — sized to headcount.
Secondary survey: history, signs, symptoms; head-to-toe inspection for deformity, bleeding, tenderness.
Record vital signs and times — the handover is only as good as the log.
Consent, dignity and communication matter as much as technique.

modules.title: Bleeding, burns & fractures
modules.focus: Catastrophic bleeding control, burn cooling rules and limb immobilization with the equipment you actually have.
keypoints: Catastrophic bleeding: direct pressure, trauma dressing, tourniquet high and tight with the time written down when pressure fails.
Burns: cool with running water 10–20 minutes, no ice, no creams, clingfilm loosely lengthways.
Fractures: immobilize as found, splint across the joints above and below, sling for elevation.
Chemical burns: brush dry powder first, then flush 20+ minutes; electrical: isolate before touch.

modules.title: Shock, environment & handover
modules.focus: Recognizing shock, the Namibian environmental trio (heat exhaustion, snakebite), and a clean patient handover.
keypoints: Shock: pale, cold, clammy, fast weak pulse — lay flat, elevate legs unless injury forbids, keep warm, nothing by mouth.
Heat exhaustion: cool shade, sips of water, active cooling; confusion means emergency.
Snakebite: immobilize the limb, pressure immobilization bandage for neurotoxic bites, no cutting, no tourniquet, no sucking; carry the patient.
Handover: ATAMIST — Age, Time, And what happened, Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment given.

quiz.q: First action for catastrophic limb bleeding:
quiz.why: Direct pressure controls most bleeding; escalate to dressing and tourniquet when pressure fails.
Cool the burn, not the patient; ice causes deeper tissue injury.
Application time drives downstream surgical decisions — write it on the skin or tag.

o: The joints above and below the fracture
quiz.why: Immobilizing the joints either side prevents the bone ends from working against each other.
The victim may still be in circuit — isolate or you join them.

o: Lay flat, elevate legs if no injury forbids
quiz.why: Elevation supports central circulation; sitting drains it further.

quiz.q: Chemical powder on skin: first brush off, then flush:
quiz.why: Dry powder activated by water burns — brush first, then long irrigation.
Cutting, sucking, tourniquets and ice all worsen outcomes; immobilize and transport.

o: Cool shade and sips of water
quiz.why: Active cooling and rehydration; confusion means escalate to emergency care.
Life first, then the systematic head-to-toe examination.

quiz.q: GN 156 first aid kits are sized by:
quiz.why: Reg. 228 scales kit contents to headcount and the nature of the work.

o: A structured sequence such as ATAMIST
quiz.why: Structure prevents the one detail the paramedic needed from being the one you forgot.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Workplace First Aid Level 1
practicum.pass_standard: All drills performed to assessor standard with correct sequencing and recording.
steps: Direct pressure and trauma bandage application on a simulated limb bleed.
Upper and lower limb fracture splinting with sling elevation performed correctly.
Burn cooling and sterile non-adherent dressing applied without contamination.
Shock positioning demonstrated with vital signs log completed accurately.
Structured patient handover delivered using the site handover format.

courses.title: SafeMan Basic Firefighting, Fire Marshal & Evacuation Commander
courses.subtitle: Theory + Live/Simulated Fire Practicum
standards: Fire Brigade Services Act 5 of 2006 (local authority)

modules.title: Fire tetrahedron & fire classes
modules.focus: What fire needs and how classes A, B, C, D and F/Electrical decide which medium fights it.
keypoints: Tetrahedron: fuel, oxygen, heat, chain reaction — break one leg and the fire dies.
Class A solids, B flammable liquids, C gases, D metals, F cooking oils; electrical fires are treated as E until isolated.
Wrong medium kills: water on oil or live electricals spreads or electrocutes.

modules.title: Extinguishers, PASS & hose/blanket
modules.focus: Selecting and operating DCP, CO2, foam and wet chemical units, plus hose reels and fire blankets.
keypoints: DCP for A/B/C and electrical; CO2 for electrical and liquid; foam for A/B; wet chemical for F.
PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep — with wind at your back and an exit behind you.
Pre-use check: gauge, pin and seal, nozzle, cylinder damage — monthly and before use.
Hose reel for A-class solids; blanket smothers pan fires and burning clothing.

modules.title: Smoke, evacuation command & roll call
modules.focus: Smoke kills before flame; the fire marshal's drill from alarm to the handover to emergency services.
keypoints: Smoke: keep low, close doors behind, never use lifts.
Marshal duties: sweep your zone, direct flow, count at assembly, report missing persons with last-seen location.
Roll call against the visitor and contractor registers, not just employees.
Handover to the fire service: what burns, who is missing, hazards and isolation status.

quiz.q: The fire tetrahedron comprises fuel, oxygen, heat and:
quiz.why: The fourth leg is the self-sustaining chemical chain reaction.
Wet chemical saponifies burning cooking oils and cools the pan.
Pull the pin, Aim low at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side.

o: With the wind in your face
Upwind with an exit at your back
quiz.why: Wind at your back drives agent into the fire and keeps escape open.

quiz.q: Live electrical fires are best met with:
quiz.why: Non-conductive media only; water conducts and foam is largely water.

quiz.q: Before using any extinguisher you check:
o: Gauge, pin and seal, nozzle, cylinder body
quiz.why: The pre-use inspection catches the unit that will fail in your hands.
Starve the flame of oxygen; keep hands protected and smother steadily.

o: Stay low and close doors behind you
quiz.why: Clean air sits low; closed doors hold back fire and smoke.

o: The attendance, visitor and contractor registers
quiz.why: Registers make visitors countable; memory forgets exactly who you need.

o: What burns, who is missing, hazards, isolations
quiz.why: The crew needs facts that change their plan: materials, people, hazards, isolation.
Water on solids; it is dangerous elsewhere.

quiz.q: A fire marshal sweeping a zone:
o: Checks rooms and closes doors while directing flow
quiz.why: The marshal's job is movement and count, not heroics; close doors, sweep, report.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Firefighting & Evacuation Command
practicum.pass_standard: Correct selection, inspection and discharge technique plus marshalling duties on live/simulated fire.
steps: Correct extinguisher selected for a live/simulated Class A, B and electrical fire scenario.
Pre-use inspection completed: gauge, pin and seal, nozzle, cylinder condition.
Windward approach with PASS discharge sweep performed safely on the training fire.
Fire blanket smothering drill demonstrated on the training pan.
Roll-call register taken and a structured emergency services briefing delivered.

courses.title: SafeMan Working at Heights & Fall Arrest Protection
courses.subtitle: Theory + Harness Practicum

modules.title: Fall physics: fall factor & clearance
modules.focus: Why fall distance, lanyard length and anchor height decide survivability before the harness is even worn.
keypoints: Fall factor = fall distance / lanyard length; FF2 (factor 2) doubles the arrest load and is never acceptable.
Clearance = fall distance + lanyard + deceleration distance + body height + safety margin; do the sum before the first step up.
Free fall is limited and shock absorbers tear out to cap arrest force near 6 kN.
Anchors above the D-ring keep fall factor at or near zero.

modules.title: Harness, lanyards & anchor points
modules.focus: Pre-use inspection discipline, 100% tie-off with twin tails, and anchor rating and placement rules.
keypoints: Full-body harness inspection: webbing (cuts, burns, chemical stains), stitching, buckles, D-rings, labels — every shift by the user and formally every period.
Twin-tail lanyards give 100% tie-off: one tail always connected while moving.
Anchor: engineered or verified 15 kN per person (per manufacturer standard), above the head where possible.
Scaffold tags: green for complete and inspected, red for incomplete or out of service — respect the tag.

modules.title: Suspension trauma & rescue plan
modules.focus: What happens in a suspended harness after arrest, and why no job goes up without a rescue plan.
keypoints: Suspension trauma: legs immobilized, blood pools, fainting and death can follow within minutes.
Relief straps or leg movement buy time; rescue must reach the casualty fast and lower them gently.
No work at height proceeds without a written rescue plan and someone on the ground who can execute it.
Post-arrest: medical assessment even when the worker feels fine.

o: The anchor is level with the D-ring
The fall distance is twice the lanyard length
quiz.why: Fall distance divided by lanyard length gives the factor; 2 is the worst case and must be designed out.

quiz.q: Maximum acceptable arrest force is capped near:
quiz.why: Shock absorbers tear stitching to keep the load on the body around 6 kN.

o: A twin-tail lanyard keeps one tail connected at all times
quiz.why: While you move, one tail is always anchored — no unprotected transitions.

o: By the user every shift before use
quiz.why: The user inspects every shift; a formal competent-person inspection supplements it.

o: Scaffold complete and inspected for use
quiz.why: Green = inspected and safe to use; red = do not use.

quiz.q: Correct clearance sum includes fall distance, lanyard, deceleration, body height and:
quiz.why: Leave a margin — hitting the level below with a stretched lanyard is a ground impact.

o: Immobility pools blood in the legs
quiz.why: Leg straps immobilize the legs; venous return fails and the casualty collapses.

o: Above the D-ring where possible and rated for the load
quiz.why: Above-head anchoring minimizes fall distance and factor; rating must be verified.

quiz.q: After a fall arrest the worker:
quiz.why: Internal injuries from arrest are invisible; assessment is mandatory.

o: Before any work at height proceeds
quiz.why: No rescue plan, no ascent — minutes decide suspension trauma outcomes.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Working at Heights
practicum.pass_standard: Inspection, donning and tie-off performed to assessor standard on the training rig.
steps: Harness webbing, stitching, buckles and D-rings inspected with faults correctly identified on the seeded example.
Harness donned with correct chest and leg strap tensioning and D-ring placement.
Twin-tail 100% tie-off progression drill completed without unprotected transitions.
Anchor point selected and justified against rating and placement rules.
Rescue plan verbal walk-through delivered for the simulated suspension scenario.

courses.title: SafeMan Confined Space Entry & Atmospheric Gas Testing
courses.subtitle: Theory + 4-Gas Practicum

modules.title: Confined spaces & their hazards
modules.focus: Definition first, then the hazard families that make confined spaces Namibia's silent killers.
keypoints: A confined space is defined by access AND hazard potential: tanks, pits, silos, vessels, trenches, big pipe.
Atmospheric hazards: oxygen deficiency/enrichment, flammable vapours, toxic gases; plus engulfment, stored product, moving machinery.
Gases stratify: heavy sink (H2S, CO2), light rise (CH4) — test top, middle, bottom.
Rescue bodies from confined spaces outnumber rescuer losses when the attendant enters — the attendant never enters.

modules.title: Gas testing & the entry permit
modules.focus: 4-gas detection discipline: bump tests, stratified sampling and the permit that gates every entry.
keypoints: Acceptable entry atmosphere: O2 19.5–23.5%, LEL <10% (work), H2S and CO below their statutory/alarm limits.
Bump test with known gas before every use; calibration on schedule; zero in fresh air.
Sampling order: top, middle, bottom, at work level and remote corners; re-test on change.
Entry permit names the space, tests, isolations, ventilation, standby, rescue plan, duration — and is signed by all parties.

modules.title: Attendant duties & non-entry rescue
modules.focus: The attendant as the lifeline and the tripod-and-winch retrieval that keeps rescuers out of the tomb.
keypoints: Attendant: constant watch, count and ID of entrants, no other duties, communication maintained, alarms on change.
Non-entry retrieval: tripod, winch, harness retrieval point rigged before entry.
Never enter for rescue without a rated atmosphere and backup — most double fatalities are would-be rescuers.
Ventilation continues while occupied; work stops when the alarm speaks.

quiz.q: Acceptable oxygen range for entry is:
quiz.why: Below 19.5% is deficient; above 23.5% raises flammability violently.

quiz.q: LEL limit for work in a confined space:
quiz.why: Work proceeds at less than 10% LEL with controls; above that the space is evacuated.

quiz.q: Gases stratify, so testing is done:
quiz.why: Heavy gases sink, light gases rise; one sample lies about the space.

o: Heavier than air and deadly at low ppm
Detectable by smell at all levels
quiz.why: Heavier than air, accumulates low; high concentrations deaden smell — never trust your nose.

o: The sensors respond to known gas
quiz.why: Expose to known concentration and check alarms fire — before every use.

o: Never enter — maintain watch and summon rescue
quiz.why: Rescuer deaths dominate confined space statistics; the attendant stays out.

o: Tests, isolations, ventilation, standby, rescue plan and duration
quiz.why: The permit is the single control document; unsigned or expired means no entry.

o: Tripod, winch and retrieval harness rigged before entry
quiz.why: Rigged before entry — after collapse it is already too late to rig.
Continuous forced ventilation keeps the atmosphere within limits; alarms override everything.
The permit's validity dies with the atmosphere; stop, exit, re-evaluate.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Confined Space Entry
practicum.pass_standard: Instrument verification, stratified sampling and permit completion to assessor standard.
steps: 4-gas detector zero and bump test verification performed and logged.
Pre-entry stratified sampling sequence (top/middle/bottom) executed with correct readings recorded.
Confined Space Entry Permit completed with isolations, ventilation and standby named.
Attendant watch established with communication and non-entry retrieval rig checked.
Permit lock-off and close-out demonstrated.

modules.title: Energy sources & the 6-step isolation
modules.focus: All the ways a machine can move, and the disciplined sequence that makes it safe to touch.
keypoints: Energy families: electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, thermal, chemical, gravitational — including stored energy in springs, accumulators and suspended loads.
6 steps: identify energy sources, notify, isolate, lock and tag, dissipate/ restrain stored energy, verify zero energy (try-out).
One worker, one lock, one key — personal locks only; a tag warns, a lock stops.
Group lockout box holds the keys; each worker applies a personal lock to the box.

modules.title: Multi-lock, tags & try-out
modules.focus: Shared isolations under group control and the physical proof that zero energy is real.
keypoints: Danger tags carry name, date, department, reason — and are never removed except by their owner per procedure.
Group boxes and hasps let many workers share one isolation with individual locks.
Try-out: attempt start controls, test with instruments, check bleeds — prove it dead before skin goes in.
Restoration is the mirror image: tools out, guards on, people clear, locks off in reverse order, notify.

quiz.q: The final LOTO step before work is:
quiz.why: Try-out proves isolation: attempt start, test, bleed — dead before skin.

o: Springs, accumulators, suspended loads, residual pressure, gravity
quiz.why: Isolation stops supply; dissipation handles what is already stored.

quiz.q: 'One worker, one lock, one key' means:
o: Each worker applies a personal lock with a unique key
quiz.why: Only the owner of the lock can remove it — that is the protection.

quiz.q: A danger tag's function is to:
o: Warn and identify — the lock does the stopping
quiz.why: Tags inform; locks physically prevent. Never confuse the two.

quiz.q: Group lockout boxes exist so that:
o: Every worker under a shared isolation holds a personal lock on the box
quiz.why: The box holds the isolation keys; the last personal lock off releases them.

o: Start-button attempt plus instrument verification and bleed checks
quiz.why: Prove it: attempt to start, measure, bleed — then and only then work.

o: By the shift boss on request
Only by their owner through procedure
quiz.why: Exception procedures exist for absence, with verification and documentation.
Raised platforms, counterweights and rams release when least expected.

o: Reverse of isolation after guards on and people clear
quiz.why: Tools out, guards on, people clear, locks off in reverse order, notify — the mirror image.
Drawings and schedules identify every energy path — missed path means live machine.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Lockout / Tagout
practicum.pass_standard: Isolation executed end-to-end on the training panel to assessor standard.
steps: All isolation points identified from the provided P&ID / switchgear diagram.
Multi-hasp and personal lock applied with a completed danger tag (name, date, reason).
Stored energy dissipated: bleed, discharge, block or lower as applicable.
Physical zero-energy try-out performed on the start controls.
Restoration sequence demonstrated in correct reverse order.

courses.title: SafeMan Task HIRA, DSTI & Toolbox Talk Facilitator
courses.subtitle: Theory + Graded Live HIRA Practicum

modules.title: Hazard vs risk & the 5×5 matrix
modules.focus: Words matter: what a hazard is, what risk adds, and scoring consequence against likelihood honestly.
keypoints: Hazard = the thing that can cause harm; risk = the chance and severity of that harm.
5×5: five consequence bands × five likelihood bands; the product bands the risk (Low / Medium / High / Extreme).
Score the realistic worst, not the common case; existing controls reduce residual risk, not the hazard.
Extreme stops work; High needs senior approval; Medium is controlled and monitored; Low is lived with.

modules.title: Task HIRA & hierarchy of controls
modules.focus: The 5-step task assessment — break the job, find the hazards, control in order, communicate, monitor.
keypoints: 5 steps: break task into steps, identify hazards per step, rate risk, apply controls in hierarchy order, communicate and monitor.
Hierarchy: elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE — descending reliability.
Controls name an owner and a check; a control nobody verifies is a hope.
Reassess when conditions, people or equipment change — the paper does not expire the risk.

modules.title: DSTI, toolbox talks & stop-work authority
modules.focus: Daily Safe Task Instructions and the 5-minute crew brief — plus the legal right to leave dangerous work.
keypoints: DSTI: today's task, hazards, controls, PPE, emergency action — signed by the crew before work.
Toolbox talk: one topic, five minutes, two-way; test understanding with questions.
Labour Act s. 42: a worker may leave a dangerous workplace without penalty when reasonable.
Facilitation: stand where all can see, invite the quiet trades, close with the commitments.

o: The thing with potential to cause harm
quiz.why: Risk adds likelihood and severity on top of the hazard's potential.
Extreme means unacceptable — stop and change the plan.

quiz.q: First choice in the hierarchy of controls:
quiz.why: Remove the hazard; controls that follow only manage it.

quiz.q: A Task HIRA is refreshed when:
quiz.why: Change invalidates yesterday's assessment — reassess on change.

o: By the crew before work starts
quiz.why: The crew's signature says they were briefed and understood today's controls.

o: One topic, five minutes, two-way with questions
quiz.why: Short, specific, interactive — comprehension beats coverage.

quiz.q: Labour Act s. 42 gives a worker the right to:
o: Leave a dangerous workplace without penalty when reasonably justified
quiz.why: The law protects the refusal of uncontrolled danger.
Inherent risk shows the raw problem; residual shows what remains with controls.
Plan for the plausible worst, not the average Tuesday.

quiz.q: A control is complete when it has:
o: An owner and a verification check
quiz.why: Ownership plus verification keeps the control alive after the meeting.

practicum.title: Assessor Practicum Checklist — Task HIRA & DSTI Facilitation
practicum.pass_standard: Graded written HIRA on a live scenario plus a facilitated crew brief.
steps: 5-step Task HIRA form completed on the assessed live work scenario with correct 5×5 scoring.
Controls mapped in hierarchy order with owners and verification named.
5-minute crew DSTI delivered covering task, hazards, controls, PPE and emergency action.
Two-way interaction demonstrated: questions asked, understanding checked.
Sign-off sheet completed and filed by the crew.

courses.title: SafeMan Hazardous Chemical Substances, GHS & Spill Control
courses.subtitle: Theory Course

modules.title: SDS 16 sections & GHS pictograms
modules.focus: Reading the safety data sheet the way it is built, and the nine GHS pictograms that headline the hazards.
keypoints: 16 sections: identification, hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, spill, handling/storage, exposure/PPE, properties, stability, toxicology, ecology, disposal, transport, regulations, other.
GHS pictograms: flame, flame-over-circle, gas cylinder, corrosion, skull, exclamation, health hazard, environment, exploding bomb.
Label elements: pictogram, signal word (Danger/Warning), hazard and precautionary statements.
The SDS lives where the chemical is used, not in a locked office.

modules.title: Segregation, drench showers & spill kits
modules.focus: Storing incompatible families apart, emergency showers and eyewash within reach, and deploying a spill kit properly.
keypoints: Segregate: oxidizers from flammables, acids from alkalis, cyanides from acids; bunding and secondary containment.
Drench showers and eyewash: within 10 seconds' travel, unobstructed, weekly flushed and logged.
Spill kit: absorbents, neutralizers, drain covers, bags, PPE — sized to the largest credible container.
Spill response: protect self, contain, stop source if safe, protect drains, notify, dispose as hazardous waste with records.

quiz.q: An SDS has how many sections?
quiz.why: GHS standardizes sixteen sections in a fixed order.
Danger for severe hazards, Warning for lesser ones.

o: Separate from alkalis and from flammables
quiz.why: Incompatibles react violently on contact — segregation is the control.

quiz.q: Drench showers must be reachable within:
quiz.why: Seconds decide chemical burn depth.

quiz.q: First action at a spill scene:
quiz.why: You are no help as a casualty; PPE first, then contain.
The circle is the oxygen donor — oxidizing substances.

quiz.q: Spill kit contents are sized to:
quiz.why: Plan for the biggest realistic release at that store.

o: 110% of the largest container's volume in the store
quiz.why: The bund catches a full failure including sprinkler/foam discharge where required.
Weekly flushing keeps lines clean and proves function.
Contaminated absorbents carry the chemical's classification; manifests keep the chain lawful.

courses.title: SafeMan Mining, Quarrying & Mineral Processing Masterclass
courses.subtitle: Sector Masterclass
standards: Ministry of Industries, Mines and Energy rules

modules.title: Mining hazards: PDS zones, blast clearance & dust
modules.focus: The interaction risks that define Namibian mining and quarrying: machines versus people, blasting, and respirable dust.
keypoints: Proximity Detection Systems (PDS) around haul trucks: exclusion zones, alerts, and never walking under a raised load.
Blast clearance: exclusion radius, sentries, clearance sign-off and re-entry only after clearance declaration.
Silica and uranium dust: engineering suppression, wet methods, respiratory protection programmes with fit testing.
Quarry faces: scaling, bench stability, stand-off distances, and the fall-of-ground discipline.

quiz.q: PDS exclusion zones exist to prevent:
quiz.why: Haul trucks have blind zones; PDS buys the seconds that sight lines cannot.

o: Only after the declared clearance and inspection
quiz.why: The clearance declaration follows inspection for misfires, fume and wall stability.

quiz.q: Silica dust control relies first on:
quiz.why: Suppress at source; PPE supports, never leads, a dust programme.
Atomic Energy and Radiation Protection Act 5 of 2005 governs NORM exposure control.

o: Loose rock from faces before work below
quiz.why: Scaled faces stop fall-of-ground before it starts.

quiz.q: Walking under a raised load is:
quiz.why: Never under a suspended or raised load — the exclusion exists because controls fail.

courses.title: SafeMan Petrochemical, Oil, Gas & Green Hydrogen Masterclass
courses.subtitle: Sector Masterclass

modules.title: Explosive zones, PSM & hydrogen/ammonia
modules.focus: Zoned areas and ignition control, the pillars of Process Safety Management, and the specific behaviours of hydrogen and ammonia.
keypoints: Zone 0/1/2 classification drives Ex-rated equipment; the permit and gas test gate every spark.
PSM pillars: process safety information, HAZOP, MOC, mechanical integrity, training, incident learning.
Hydrogen: wide flammability range, invisible flame, high leak rate — detectors and bond/earth discipline.
Ammonia: toxic and refrigerant-cold; water spray for knockdown, escape sets, and never entering a cloud.

quiz.q: Zone 1 is where an explosive atmosphere:
quiz.why: Zone 0 continuous, 1 likely in normal operation, 2 only in abnormal/short periods.

o: Structured process hazard study using guide words
quiz.why: Guide words (No, More, Less, Reverse...) applied to design intent expose deviations.
Low-luminosity flame — approach with detectors, not eyesight.

o: Every technical/organizational change for new hazards
quiz.why: Unreviewed change is how safe plants drift into unsafe ones.

o: Avoid entry, use water spray knockdown and escape sets
quiz.why: Toxic and cryogenic — trained teams, knockdown from upwind, no unprotected entry.

o: Prevent the equipment igniting the zone atmosphere
quiz.why: Containment/limitation of ignition sources matched to the zone classification.

courses.title: SafeMan Construction, Civil & Electrical Contractors Masterclass
courses.subtitle: Sector Masterclass

modules.title: Excavations, lifting & the contractor SHE file
modules.focus: Ground, cranes and paperwork: the three things that decide whether a Namibian site week ends well.
keypoints: Excavations: support/shoring or battering by soil class, access ladders every 7.5 m, spoil 1 m back, inspection after rain.
Lifting: registered operators, load charts, exclusion zones, lift plans for tandem/critical lifts, registered lifting tackle with colour-coded inspection.
Contractor SHE file: policy, risk assessments, method statements, appointments, medicals, training records, emergency plan — vetted before mobilization.
Electrical: permit-to-work, isolation and earth, test-before-touch, underground service clearance before digging.

quiz.q: Spoil heaps stand back from an excavation edge at least:
quiz.why: Spoil adds surcharge and slides back in — keep it a metre back minimum.

quiz.q: Ladder access in excavations is placed:
o: Within every 7.5 m of travel for workers
quiz.why: Escape must be within a few seconds' reach anywhere in the trench.

o: A written lift plan with exclusions and roles
quiz.why: Critical/tandem lifts get engineered lift plans before the crane starts.

quiz.q: Lifting tackle inspection is shown by:
quiz.why: Colour coding makes overdue tackle visible at a glance.

o: Clear and mark underground services and use safe dig practice
quiz.why: Service strikes kill and black out sites; locate, mark, hand-dig near the line.

quiz.q: The contractor SHE file is vetted:
quiz.why: The gate is before mobilization — after the fact is an audit, not a control.
